entries.concept: IAM least privilege and access analysis
entries.description: IAM policies should grant only the minimum actions required. Example: allow s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on specific bucket ARN only. Use IAM Access Analyzer to find unused permissions: aws accessanalyzer create-analyzer --type ACCOUNT. Generate policies from CloudTrail activity: aws iam generate-service-last-accessed-details.
decision_rules: Start with deny-all and add only required actions on specific resources (not Action: '*')
Run IAM Access Analyzer to detect overly broad permissions quarterly
Use IAM Access Advisor to remove permissions unused for 90+ days
tradeoffs: Fine-grained IAM policies require more maintenance as application requirements change
anti_patterns: Action: '*' or Resource: '*' in production IAM policies
Using the AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy for application roles
Long-lived IAM access keys — use IAM roles and temporary credentials
aws_alignment: Enable IAM Access Analyzer for every AWS account
Use AWS Organizations SCPs to prevent privilege escalation across accounts

entries.concept: Encryption at rest and in transit with KMS
entries.description: Create dedicated KMS keys per environment with enable_key_rotation=true and deletion_window_in_days=30. Apply SSE-KMS to S3 buckets with bucket_key_enabled=true for cost optimization. Enforce TLS 1.2+ for all data in transit.
decision_rules: Create one KMS key per environment (dev/staging/prod) — do not share keys across environments
Enable automatic key rotation (enable_key_rotation=true) on all KMS keys
Enable bucket_key_enabled=true on S3 SSE-KMS to reduce KMS API call costs
tradeoffs: SSE-KMS adds latency compared to SSE-S3 — acceptable for sensitive data, consider SSE-S3 for high-throughput non-sensitive data
anti_patterns: Using the AWS-managed key (aws/s3) instead of a customer-managed KMS key — no key rotation control
Transmitting data over HTTP in production — enforce TLS via bucket policies and ALB listeners
aws_alignment: Use aws_kms_key with deletion_window_in_days >= 7 and enable_key_rotation = true

entries.description: Three-tier VPC: public subnets (ALB only, map_public_ip_on_launch=false), private app subnets (ECS/EKS), private data subnets (RDS). Use at least 2 AZs. Route private subnets through NAT Gateway. Use VPC Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB to avoid NAT Gateway costs.
decision_rules: Place ALB in public subnets, application workloads in private app subnets, databases in private data subnets
Never assign public IPs to EC2, ECS tasks, or RDS instances directly
Use VPC Endpoints (Gateway type for S3/DynamoDB, Interface for other services) to keep traffic on the AWS network
tradeoffs: NAT Gateway costs ~$35/month per AZ — use VPC Endpoints to reduce egress costs for high-volume AWS API traffic
anti_patterns: Placing RDS or ElastiCache in public subnets
Using a single NAT Gateway for multi-AZ deployments — creates an availability bottleneck
aws_alignment: Use aws_vpc_endpoint for S3 and DynamoDB (Gateway type — free)
Deploy NAT Gateways in each AZ for high-availability outbound internet access from private subnets

entries.description: Configure CloudTrail with is_multi_region_trail=true, include_global_service_events=true, enable_log_file_validation=true, KMS encryption, and S3 data event logging. Delivers comprehensive audit trail of all API activity across all regions.
decision_rules: Enable a multi-region trail — a single-region trail misses global service events (IAM, STS)
Enable log file validation to detect tampering of delivered log files
Encrypt CloudTrail logs with a dedicated KMS key (separate from application keys)
tradeoffs: CloudTrail logs for S3 data events generate high volume — filter to specific buckets to control costs
anti_patterns: Disabling CloudTrail or limiting it to a single region
Storing CloudTrail logs in the same account and bucket without separate S3 access controls — logs could be tampered by a compromised account
aws_alignment: Use a dedicated Log Archive account in AWS Organizations for CloudTrail logs
Enable AWS Config to detect CloudTrail being disabled (cloud-trail-enabled rule)

entries.description: Enable GuardDuty with S3 log analysis, Kubernetes audit log analysis, and EBS malware protection. GuardDuty uses ML and threat intelligence to detect anomalous API calls, crypto mining, compromised credentials, and lateral movement.
decision_rules: Enable GuardDuty in every AWS account and every region
Enable all three data sources: s3_logs, kubernetes audit_logs, malware_protection for EBS
Set up SNS notifications or EventBridge rules to alert on HIGH/CRITICAL findings
tradeoffs: GuardDuty pricing is based on data volume analyzed — S3 data events can be costly for high-traffic buckets
anti_patterns: Not enabling GuardDuty — leaves the account without automated threat detection
Enabling GuardDuty without acting on findings — security theater
aws_alignment: Use AWS Security Hub to aggregate GuardDuty findings with other security services
Enable GuardDuty at the AWS Organizations level via delegated administrator

entries.description: Attach AWS WAFv2 WebACL to ALB or API Gateway. Configure rate limiting rule (2000 requests per 5 minutes per IP) and AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet (OWASP Top 10 protections). Enable CloudWatch metrics and sampled request logging for visibility.
decision_rules: Attach WAF to every public-facing ALB or API Gateway endpoint
Start with AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and add custom rules for application-specific needs
Set rate_based_statement limit at 2000/5-min as a starting baseline — tune based on traffic patterns
tradeoffs: WAF managed rules may produce false positives for legitimate traffic — use Count mode before switching to Block
WAF adds latency (~1ms) — negligible for most workloads
anti_patterns: Exposing ALBs or API Gateways to the internet without WAF
Using WAF in Count mode permanently — rules do not block malicious traffic
aws_alignment: Use AWS Shield Standard (included) for DDoS protection at L3/L4
Add AWS Shield Advanced for volumetric DDoS protection on critical endpoints

entries.description: Minimum security baseline for all AWS accounts: MFA on all IAM users (especially root), no root access keys, automatic KMS key rotation, S3 bucket versioning and public access block, CloudTrail enabled all regions, GuardDuty enabled, Security Hub with CIS standards, Config Rules configured, VPC Flow Logs enabled, TLS 1.2+ enforced, secrets in Secrets Manager (not env vars).
decision_rules: Enforce this checklist for every new AWS account before deploying any workloads
Use AWS Security Hub CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark to track compliance automatically
anti_patterns: Storing secrets in EC2 userdata, Lambda environment variables, or SSM Parameter Store Standard (not encrypted by default)
Not enabling MFA on AWS root account — single point of compromise for entire account
aws_alignment: Use AWS Organizations SCPs to enforce this baseline across all member accounts
Use AWS Config conformance packs (Operational Best Practices for CIS) for automated compliance
